bib.title: Think Bayes, ch. 1: Bayes's Theorem
bib.venue: book chapter (Think Bayes, 1st ed., Green Tea Press / O'Reilly, 2012; no journal)

question: How does conditional probability lead to Bayes's theorem, and how is it used as a table of prior, likelihood and posterior?

results.claim: Cookie problem: a vanilla cookie raises Bowl 1 from 1/2 to 3/5.
results.setup: Bowl 1 has 30 vanilla and 10 chocolate; Bowl 2 has 20 of each; bowl chosen at random

results.claim: p(D) is 5/8 by the law of total probability over the two bowls.
M&M problem table: yellow from the 1994 bag and green from the 1996 bag gives posterior 20/27 for hypothesis A.
results.setup: 1994 mix 20% yellow, 10% green; 1996 mix 14% yellow, 20% green; one M&M drawn from each of two bags

results.claim: Likelihoods may be scaled by any common factor because it cancels in the normalisation.
results.setup: mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive suite
results.quote: you can multiply the likelihoods by any factor, if it is convenient

results.claim: Monty Hall: switching wins with probability 2/3, sticking 1/3.
results.setup: Monty picks uniformly between B and C when the car is behind A; data = Monty opens B and no car is there

results.claim: If Monty always opens B when he can, opening B tells you nothing: posteriors 1/2 and 1/2 for A and C.

limits: Textbook level; the 2012 first edition, code in Python 2; the chapter has no empirical results.
practices: Make hypotheses mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive (a suite) so the normalising constant is a sum (p.6).
Fill a Prior / Likelihood / p(H)p(D|H) / Posterior table; the likelihood of the data decides everything, so re-derive it when the data-generating process changes (p.9-10).

terms.definition: a set of hypotheses that are mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive
Bayes's theorem as a way to update the probability of a hypothesis H in light of data D over time

lineage.note: Bayes's theorem as conditional probability; Wikipedia cookie example
